items.title: Mock 2 — Retell Lecture Q1 (Listening to cracking knees)
items.transcript: The sound of a cracking knee isn't particularly pleasant. But it gets worse when you listen up close. "It does for most people. But for me, it actually just makes me excited." Omer Inan, an electrical engineer at Georgia Tech. "I actually feel like there's some real information in them that can be exploited for the purposes of helping people with rehab." Inan's experience with cracking knees goes back to his days as an undergrad at Stanford, where he threw discus. "If I had a really hard workout, then the next day, of course, I'd be sore, but I'd also sometimes feel this basically catching or popping or creaking every now and then in my knee." A few years later, he found himself building tiny microphones at a high-end audio company. So when he got to Georgia Tech and heard the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, DARPA, wanted better tech for knee injuries, he thought: why not strap tiny microphones to people's knees, to eavesdrop as their legs bend? "What we think it is, is the cartilage and bone rubbing against each other, the surfaces inside the knee rubbing against each other, during those movements." He and a team of physiologists and engineers built a prototype with stretchy athletic tape and a few tiny mics and skin sensors. And preliminary tests on athletes suggest the squishy sounds the device picks up are more erratic, and more irregular, in an injured knee than in a healthy one. Which Inan says might allow patients and doctors to track healing after surgery. Details appear in the IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. "The primary application we're targeting at first is to give people a decision aid during rehabilitation, following an acute knee injury, to help them understand when they can perform particular activities, and when they can move to different intensities of particular activities." A useful thing to take a crack at.
keyPoints: The sound of a cracking knee isn't pleasant.
But there's real information in sound that can help people with rehab.
Strap tiny microphones to people's knees.
The sounds the device receives are more irregular in an injured knee.
This allows doctors to track healing after surgery.

items.title: Mock 2 — Retell Lecture Q2 (Raising bilingual children)
items.transcript:
Many parents communicate and educate their children with two languages, probably because they both know more than one language, or they come from different countries.

Most of these parents think this can benefit their children's language learning.

But actually kids will get confused when their parents use different languages from each other to describe the same object.

If one parent sticks to one language, and the other one sticks to another language, their children will not be confused any more.

items.title: Mock 2 — Retell Lecture Q3 (Searching for other cosmic civilizations)
items.transcript: The possibility of the existence of other cosmic civilizations has always been an important topic in space research. Scientists are interested in finding out whether life exists on other planets beyond Earth and whether another civilization could develop somewhere in the universe. Every year, around 7 stars are created in some areas of the universe, and there are many planets formed around these stars. However, most planets around them cannot support life because their environments are usually either too hot or too cold. Researchers estimate that only about 20% of all planets may meet all necessary criteria and have a chance to have life. Even if a planet has suitable conditions, the possibility of life developing into a complex civilization is still very small. The change of appearance of life from simple organisms to advanced civilizations is extremely rare, which makes it hard to find another cosmic civilization. Therefore, although the universe contains countless planets, discovering another intelligent civilization remains a great challenge.
